opus-5.5.text:
I think the shift changes the competition in a fairly fundamental way.

In the pretraining era, the game was mostly about scale. Who has more compute, who can collect and clean more data, who can run a stable training job on tens of thousands of cards. Those things still matter a lot, but they're increasingly becoming the entry ticket rather than the differentiator. Once several teams have a strong enough base model, the base itself starts to look somewhat similar across labs.

Post-training, especially reinforcement learning, is where the gaps open up again, and in a less predictable way. It's much more about taste and iteration speed. How do you design the reward? Which tasks do you choose to train on? How do you build environments where the model can actually explore and get verifiable feedback? These aren't problems you solve by just adding more GPUs. A small team with good intuition can sometimes move faster than a big team that's still thinking in pretraining terms.

It also changes the rhythm. Pretraining is like a big bet every few months: you commit, you wait, you see what you got. Post-training is much tighter. You can try an idea, see results within days, and keep compounding. So the organizations that win are the ones that can turn research ideas into experiments very quickly and are willing to throw away things that don't work.

And honestly, I think it makes the competition more open. The base model sets the ceiling, but how close you get to that ceiling, and in which directions, like reasoning, coding, agentic tasks, really depends on post-training. That's where a lot of creativity is happening right now, and it means the leaderboard can change faster than people expect.

r001.rationale: The response says post-training enables experiments and iteration within days, compared with pretraining’s larger bets every few months. It does not clearly connect that faster pace to releasing models more often.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the most important change is that the entry ticket for the game has come down, but what it takes to actually win has gotten more complicated, not less.

In the pretraining era, the competition was fundamentally about scale. Who had more compute, more data, more patience to run a single giant job for months. The recipe was relatively clear, and the differentiation came from execution and resources. If you were a smaller team, you could watch from the sidelines, but you couldn't really play.

Post-training changes that in a few ways. First, the compute per experiment is much smaller, so iteration speed matters more than raw budget. You can run many RL experiments in the time it takes to do one pretraining run, which means a team of twenty very good people can discover things that a team of two hundred misses. Second, the open-source base models are now good enough that the base model is no longer the moat it used to be. Everyone is starting from a similar floor.

But I want to push back on the idea that this makes competition easier. The hard part has shifted from "can you train the model" to "do you know what you want the model to become, and can you measure it." Reward design, data curation, understanding where the model actually fails versus where your benchmark says it fails. That is a much more taste-driven problem. It rewards teams that are genuinely close to real usage and have strong research intuition, rather than teams that simply have the most GPUs.

So I'd summarize it this way: pretraining competition was a war of resources, and post-training competition is more like a war of judgment. The number of credible players has gone up, but the gap between the teams that understand the models deeply and the ones that are just copying recipes will become more visible, not less. And frankly, I think that is healthier for the field.

r001.rationale: The response says post-training allows faster experimentation and iteration than pretraining, but does not identify a faster model-release cadence.

astra-6.text:
I think competition is shifting from who can build the strongest base model to who can turn that foundation into a system that learns and performs reliably on real tasks.

Pretraining is still important—it provides much of the model’s underlying capability. But post-training changes where teams can differentiate. It puts more weight on the quality of feedback, the tasks you choose, and whether you can evaluate success accurately. More training doesn’t necessarily help if the reward is measuring the wrong thing.

That also changes the role of data. You need more than a large collection of examples; you need useful learning signals, especially around the model’s failures. In areas where results can be checked clearly, that feedback loop can be very powerful. For more open-ended tasks, defining what counts as a good answer remains difficult.

So I wouldn’t say this shift makes compute or scale irrelevant. It makes the competition more multidimensional. The advantage increasingly comes from connecting a strong base model with good training methods, reliable evaluation, and feedback from actual use.

r001.rationale: The response describes post-training as a way to differentiate through feedback, task choice, and evaluation, but does not say it enables faster model releases than pretraining.

sol-6.1.text:
I think competition is shifting from who can build the strongest foundation to who can turn that foundation into the most useful capabilities. Pretraining still matters—it gives you the starting point. But post-training increasingly determines whether a model can reason reliably, use tools, and handle a complex task from beginning to end.

That changes where the hard work is. It’s not simply about collecting more data. You need to define what a good result looks like, build environments where the model can learn, and provide feedback that actually rewards progress. For tasks with clear answers, that’s relatively straightforward. For open-ended tasks, evaluating quality becomes a central challenge.

So I don’t see post-training as making pretraining irrelevant. The two reinforce each other. But I do think competition becomes more dynamic: a strong base model creates an opportunity, and the quality of the learning process after pretraining determines how much of that opportunity you can realize.

r001.rationale: The response says post-training makes competition more dynamic, but does not identify it as enabling models to be released faster than pretraining.
